$comment: Shared conformance vectors for the gcache JSON value envelope.
Read by BOTH tests/test_conformance.py and go/conformance_test.go. Neither may hardcode a
case: one source of truth is the point, so a reader that diverges fails instead of passing
against its own mirrored copy. Parity used to be hand-mirrored literals in suites that ran
in separate repositories, where nothing could run both sides; five cross-language claims
went silently false in one afternoon under that arrangement.
expect=accept means decode succeeds AND yields `decoded`. expect=reject means the reader
must treat the value as a MISS -- an exception the client converts to 'miss', never a
partial or defaulted value. A reject case with a plausible payload is deliberate: a reader
that ignores the invalid field and returns the payload anyway must fail here.
A vector may carry `rejectedBy`/`acceptedBy` when the clients DELIBERATELY differ, meaning
one cannot represent the value faithfully and rejecting it there yields a miss-and-rewrite
rather than two clients serving the same bytes as different numbers. `asymmetryIsSafe` must
say why that direction is the safe one. A suite asserts only its own client's side.

vectors.name: canonical
vectors.why: The shape both writers emit. If this fails nothing else matters.

vectors.name: whole-number-float-timestamps
vectors.why: 1757308800123.0 IS a whole number of milliseconds. Rejecting every float would be over-strict, and this vector is what keeps the is_integer/isInteger check from degenerating into that.

vectors.name: fractional-expires
vectors.why: Found in review, not by a test. TS kept the fraction and Python rounded; both compare against a threshold, so expiresAtMs=x.9 at now=x is a HIT in one client and EXPIRED in the other. Same bytes, opposite answers -- so both must reject.

vectors.name: fractional-created
vectors.why: Same divergence on the other field, which feeds `watermark_ms >= createdAtMs` rather than expiry. Both fields need the vector; fixing one and not the other passed a single-field test.

vectors.name: negative-fractional-created
vectors.why: int() truncates toward zero and floor does not, so the two rounding strategies disagree in OPPOSITE directions for a negative value. That sign dependence is why rounding was the wrong fix at all.

vectors.name: version-zero
vectors.why: Not the current version, so not readable. Pinned because `version` was once checked truthily, which accepted 0.

vectors.name: version-true
vectors.why: JSON true is not 1. Python's `version != 1` is False for True because bool is an int subclass, so it was ACCEPTED there and rejected in TS -- a divergence with no symptom until a foreign writer produced one.

vectors.name: created-at-string
vectors.why: A timestamp as a string is the most likely shape from a hand-written or foreign entry. Must be a miss, not a coerced number.

vectors.name: expires-beyond-double
vectors.why: A 401-digit integer literal. JSON.parse maps it to Infinity so TS rejected it, while Python's arbitrary-precision int accepted it happily -- and an entry with an impossible expiry never looks expired AND can never satisfy watermark_ms >= createdAtMs, so no invalidation can ever reach it.

vectors.name: base64-payload
vectors.why: The bytes path. Python base64s a bytes payload where Go never does, so this is the one encoding both must agree on.

vectors.name: unknown-encoding
vectors.why: An encoding neither client implements must miss rather than being read as utf8.

vectors.name: payload-not-a-string
vectors.why: The payload is a JSON string carrying serialized bytes, never a nested object. A reader that accepts an object here would re-serialize it differently from the writer.

vectors.name: missing-expires
vectors.why: An absent expiry is not an infinite one.

vectors.name: not-json-at-all
vectors.why: Garbage in the keyspace must be a miss, never an exception that escapes the read path -- a cache must not be able to fail a request.

vectors.name: created-above-2-53
vectors.why: The silent-disagreement case. Go's decodeEnvelope takes the field into a float64 and rounds 9007199254740993 to ...992; Python's json.loads returns the exact int. So in the 2^53..int64 band both clients ACCEPTED and then compared a different number against the staleness threshold, with no error anywhere -- worse than a miss, which heals on the next read. Both now stop at 2^53.

vectors.name: created-at-max-safe-integer
vectors.why: The boundary itself, so the safe-integer bound cannot drift into rejecting the largest faithfully-representable value. 9007199254740991 is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and every client reads it exactly. Mutation-checked in Go too: making the boundary exclusive rejects this vector.

vectors.name: base64-unpadded
vectors.why: A raw encoder emits no padding. Python's b64decode rejects it, so without the shared re-padding step the same entry is a Go hit and a Python miss-and-rewrite.

vectors.name: base64-url-safe-alphabet
vectors.why: base64.RawURLEncoding and urlsafe_b64encode emit - and _. Python's b64decode rejects both, so each client must map them onto the standard alphabet first.

vectors.name: base64-line-wrapped
vectors.why: The base64 CLI wraps at 76 columns, so an entry repaired by hand carries newlines. Whitespace must be stripped BEFORE padding is computed: padding a length that counts the newlines decoded for one client only when that length happened to be a multiple of four.

$comment: What each client renders for a key PREFIX, recorded rather than asserted, so a change to
either side fails here instead of becoming silently unshared entries. Both clients agree on
every case; the percent-encoding divergence these cases were written for is gone with the
client that had it.

argOrdering.$comment: Argument ORDER is not part of the wire key: both clients sort by name, byte-ordinal and stable. Recorded because no multi-arg vector existed, which let Go sort while Python's constructor did not -- the same call built two different Redis entries. Values are MEASURED from each client, not asserted.

cases.name: reverse-alpha
cases.why: The case that caught a real divergence, and the only shape that can. Go sorted args and Python's constructor did not, so the same call built two different Redis entries. No multi-arg vector existed, which is why it survived review. Every writer of a real key sorts -- cached() before constructing, and Go's ValueKey -- so the sorted rendering IS the existing wire format.

cases.name: already-alpha
cases.why: The control, and a warning. It renders identically whether a client sorts or preserves input order, so a corpus of only alphabetical cases proves nothing. Meaningful only paired with reverse-alpha.

cases.name: duplicate-names
cases.why: Two args sharing a name. Order is the only thing distinguishing them, so an UNSTABLE sort reorders them and changes the key. All three sorts are stable.

cases.name: single-arg
cases.why: One arg cannot expose an ordering bug. Present so a suite that silently skips the multi-arg cases still has something to fail on.

$comment: Why the watermark keeps an int64 bound while envelope timestamps stop at 2^53.
Not an oversight, and not inherited -- measured. The two fields reach Python through
DIFFERENT parsers:
envelope   json.loads  -> an exact Python int at any magnitude
watermark  float()     -> a float64, so it rounds above 2^53, exactly as Go and
JavaScript do
Measured in Python at this revision:
CORRECTION, found by the cases below when they were first asserted: the watermark values
are NOT identical to Go's. Go's parseWatermark tries ParseInt BEFORE ParseFloat, so an
integer-formatted watermark is exact at any int64 magnitude:
The divergence is unreachable rather than harmless-by-luck, and that is the part worth
keeping. Staleness is `watermark_ms >= created_at_ms`, and BOTH clients cap created_at at
2^53-1 on read, so any watermark at or above 2^53 exceeds every createdAtMs either client
will accept -- the two answer 'stale' together no matter which side of the rounding they
landed on. Write-back is suppressed for both for the same reason. So the numbers differ
and no decision does.
This is why the section is asserted now: it previously said the opposite, in prose no
suite read, and the claim would have been used to justify a change to one of the parsers.
Consequence to know before anyone 'fixes' this: within Python, above 2^53, a rounded
watermark is compared against an exact created_at, so `watermark_ms >= created_at_ms`
can be off by one millisecond. Unreachable in practice -- 2^53 ms is year 287396 -- and
now doubly so, since the envelope side rejects those values outright. Do not align the
two parsers without re-measuring Go first.
The cases below are the measured triples above, asserted rather than recited. Prose in
this file that no suite reads is a comment with extra steps -- the watermarkTiming
section was exactly that until a mutation showed the numbers it 'pinned' were free.

cases.name: just-above-2^53
cases.why: float64 cannot represent it, so Python rounds down; Go's ParseInt keeps it exact.

cases.name: two-above-2^53
cases.why: Python rounds the OTHER way here, so a test using only the first case would pass on a floor().

cases.name: 2^53-minus-one
cases.why: The last exactly-representable value: both agree, and the envelope still accepts it. Pins where the divergence starts.

_why: hash_component / HashComponent must agree byte for byte or a component hashed by one
client is unfindable by the other -- a cache that writes fine and never hits, with no
error on either side. Lowercase hex of SHA-256 over the UTF-8 bytes.
A lone surrogate is absent on purpose: Python raises UnhashableKeyComponent while Go
hashes whatever bytes it holds, so there IS no agreed answer. See that exception.

cases._why: the empty string is well defined and both clients agree; whether it is MEANINGFUL is the caller's call
the shape this exists for -- PII that must not sit in a key in the clear
non-ASCII and the key delimiter: hashing happens BEFORE rendering, so a colon in the input cannot split a component
long input: the digest is fixed width, which is why hashing retires the byte bound

_why: The PROTO framing, byte for byte. Hand-written in both clients (four fields is too
small to justify putting protoc in this repo), so nothing but these vectors stops
the two from drifting -- and a drift here is silent: one client writes an entry the
other cannot read, with no error on the write side.
firstByteRange is the load-bearing part. A tag byte is (field << 3) | wire_type, so
fields 1-14 over proto3's wire types span 0x08..0x75 -- disjoint from JSON's '{'
(0x7b) and pickle's 0x80. Field 16 with a varint IS 0x80, which is why the schema
may never use a field number above 14.

canonical.why: One fully-specified entry. Both clients must produce these exact bytes.

rejects.name: version-too-new
rejects.why: version 99 > what this reader knows. GREATER than, not !=: an added field must not be a flag day.

rejects.name: no-version
rejects.why: field 1 absent. An unversioned entry was not written by any gcache client.

rejects.name: payload-runs-past-the-end
rejects.why: truncated in transit: the length prefix outruns the buffer.

rejects.name: group-wire-type
rejects.why: wire type 3 is a proto2 group. proto3 never emits one, so no client wrote this.

rejects.name: proto-negative-created
rejects.why: created_at_ms is int64 in the schema, so a negative encodes as a 10-byte two's-complement varint. Python read it as UNSIGNED and got 18446744073709551615 while Go read -1: the same bytes, two values. A negative epoch-ms is not a timestamp either way.

rejects.name: proto-negative-expires
rejects.why: the dangerous half: a plausible created_at with a negative expiry. Read as unsigned it is ~584 million years in the future, so the entry never expires and is served as a fresh hit forever -- on one client only.

rejects.name: proto-varint-wider-than-64-bits
rejects.why: a ten-byte varint whose tenth byte exceeds 0x01 encodes past uint64. Go WRAPS it, Python keeps it, so the same bytes decode to different numbers -- and after signed conversion it lands as a large POSITIVE value that sails past the negative-timestamp guard.

rejects.name: proto-varint-wider-than-64-bits-in-version
rejects.why: the over-width varint in VERSION rather than a timestamp. In created_at_ms the wrapped value comes out as -2^63 and the negative-timestamp guard rejects it first, so that vector never reached the varint guard on the Go side -- it passed with the guard deleted. Here nothing else catches it: without the guard Go wraps the version to 1 and returns a HIT while Python refuses the same bytes.

$comment: The three numbers the resurrection invariant rests on, declared by hand in each
language: constants.py and go/cache.go. Nothing compared them before -- setting
WATERMARK_TTL_SECONDS to 6h left all 268 Python tests green, because every test is
written relative to the constants and therefore holds for any pair of numbers.
The invariant: a watermark must outlive every entry it can suppress, so
maxTrackedTtlSeconds + maxFutureBufferSeconds <= watermarkTtlSeconds
and the two caps are enforced locally -- the write path against the TTL, invalidate
against the buffer -- so neither party needs the other's number at call time.
Python writing a 6h watermark while Go assumes 5h breaks the argument in BOTH
directions and nothing else would report it.
Payloads the two clients would decode to DIFFERENT values, and near-misses that they
must both accept. Refused on write (encode_json / encodeEnvelope) and on read, so a
poisoned entry from a foreign writer degrades to the fallback instead of being served.
The hazard is the ESCAPE form. json.dumps with ensure_ascii writes U+D800 as the six
ASCII characters \ud800, so the stored envelope is pure ASCII and Go's utf8.Valid gate
cannot see it -- the surrogate only reappears when the CALLER's codec unescapes the
payload. Python then returns a str holding U+D800 and Go substitutes U+FFFD. Both
clients report a hit, nothing raises, no metric moves.
The accepts matter as much as the rejects. Two earlier versions of this rule were
regexes and each was wrong in a different direction: the first refused every emoji,
because a valid surrogate PAIR is also two escapes; the second refused ordinary text
containing the characters \ud800, because an escaped backslash makes \\ud800 and the
pattern matched from the second one.
The two clients answer this with DIFFERENT mechanisms and must still agree. Python asks
json.loads and re-dumps without ensure_ascii; Go's encoding/json substitutes rather
than erroring, so it walks the escapes instead. That is what this section is for.
The last three cases are where the two mechanisms diverged on inputs the first eight did
not reach, each found by running both implementations over the same strings:
duplicate keys   json.loads kept only the LAST, so the surrogate left the parsed tree
and Python accepted what Go's escape scan refused. Fixed with
object_pairs_hook=list, which also makes the walk visit keys.
NaN              json.loads accepts it by default and Go's json.Valid does not, so the
two disagreed about whether the payload was JSON at all, and therefore
about whether this rule applied. Fixed with parse_constant.
Both needed a writer other than JsonSerializer, which is why nothing else caught them.

cases.name: lone-high-escape
cases.why: The escape form, from any serializer using ensure_ascii.

cases.name: lone-low-escape
cases.why: The low half alone. An early matcher covered [89ab] only and let this through.

cases.name: lone-high-escape-uppercase
cases.why: JSON permits \uD800 as readily as \ud800, so a case-sensitive gate misses half of them.

cases.name: trailing-high-escape
cases.why: A high surrogate with nothing after it. The pair lookahead must not run off the end.

cases.name: valid-surrogate-pair
cases.why: An emoji under ensure_ascii. Refusing these was the first version's bug.

cases.name: escaped-backslash-then-text
cases.why: A literal backslash followed by the characters ud800 -- prose about unicode, or JSON inside JSON. Refusing it was the second version's bug.

cases.name: no-surrogate
cases.why: The common payload, which must not pay a parse.

cases.name: not-json
cases.why: Neither client unescapes a non-JSON payload, so neither can disagree about it.

cases.name: duplicate-key-hides-the-surrogate
cases.why: A later duplicate must not launder an earlier surrogate out of the payload.

cases.name: non-strict-json-nan
cases.why: NaN is not JSON. Both clients must agree this payload is outside the rule, not just both end at a miss.

cases.name: surrogate-in-a-key
cases.why: A key diverges exactly as a value does, and a walk over .values() alone misses it.

$comment: An EXPLICIT nesting limit, counted identically in both clients, replacing each parser's
own private one. Built rather than stored, because a 4000-deep payload has no business in
this file.
The limit exists for determinism, not safety. Go's scanner stops at 10000 and CPython's
depends on the interpreter's stack -- depth 4000 parsed on a laptop and raised
RecursionError in CI, so the same payload was written on one host and refused on another.
Two Python pods disagreeing about an entry is the same defect as Python and Go disagreeing
about one, and a test caught it only because CI happened to have the smaller stack.
Past the limit both clients refuse, which is the closed direction: a payload this client
cannot inspect must not be served. It is only ever reached by a payload that already
contains a surrogate escape, since the substring gate runs first.
The count is NET depth and skips brackets inside string literals, so a flat array of 600
objects and a value containing the characters '[[[[' both stay under it. A raw count of
'[' and '{' would refuse the first of those.

cases.why: The ordinary case, nowhere near the limit.
Just inside: still inspected, and the surrogate is found.
Exactly at the limit, which is inclusive. Pins which side the boundary falls on.
Just past: refused for being uninspectable rather than for the surrogate. Both are a refusal, so the reason strings matter and both clients emit the same one.
The depth that used to parse on a laptop and raise RecursionError in CI.
Past Go's own scanner limit too. Previously the one recorded disagreement; the shared limit removed it.

$comment: A tracked entry stamped far enough ahead is immune to invalidation, in both clients.
Staleness is `watermarkMs >= createdAtMs` and a watermark carries a real clock time, so
it never reaches a stamp far enough ahead -- while the expiry guard passes (expiresAtMs
is ahead too) and the lifetime guard passes (the declared lifetime is legal). The entry
survives every invalidate call for its whole Redis TTL.
Clock-relative, so these are offsets rather than bytes: each suite builds an envelope at
now + createdAtOffsetSeconds and reads it back.
boundSeconds is maxFutureBufferSeconds, and that is the whole derivation: an invalidation
issued NOW writes a watermark of at most now + maxFutureBuffer, so an entry created at or
before that instant is still suppressible and one created after it is not. The accepts are
as load-bearing as the rejects -- a guard refusing the reachable side would turn a
one-millisecond clock lead into a permanent miss-and-rewrite loop.

cases.name: inside-the-frontier
cases.why: A watermark written now with the full buffer can still reach it, so it is served.

cases.name: past-the-frontier
cases.why: No watermark any invalidation can write now reaches this stamp.

cases.name: a-year-ahead
cases.why: The shape a broken clock or a foreign writer actually produces.

cases.name: untracked-past-the-frontier
cases.why: No watermark to be out of reach of, so refusing it costs a skewed writer its hit rate and buys nothing.
